claims.text: The equiatomic Cr–Mn–Fe–Co–Ni alloy and the compared equiatomic quaternary and ternary subsets are single-phase FCC after thermomechanical processing.
Changing from the quinary alloy to its quaternary and ternary subsets alters local chemical short-range order and possible solute clustering.
Altered solute interactions drive the proposed differences in local chemical short-range order.
Differences in chemical short-range order modify stacking-fault energies.
Differences in chemical short-range order modify dislocation mobility.
Chemical short-range order and solute clustering influence the activation of partial dislocations and deformation twinning.
The quinary alloy's greater chemical complexity increases the likelihood of local ordering or clustering.
Local ordering or clustering in the quinary alloy raises barriers to dislocation glide.
Higher barriers to dislocation glide delay plastic instability in the quinary alloy.
Reducing the constituent count reduces local chemical fluctuations and lowers barriers to dislocation motion.
Lower barriers to dislocation motion cause earlier localized deformation, lower strain hardening, and lower ductility.
Relative to the quinary baseline, the quaternary alloys will have lower strain-hardening rates, reduced uniform elongation, and earlier plastic localization.
The predicted reductions in strain hardening and uniform elongation will be especially pronounced in the ternary alloys.
Constituent count alone is inadequate to explain the alloys' differing deformation and failure behavior.
The proposed comparison holds thermomechanical processing, tensile-test temperature, strain rate, and FCC phase constitution approximately constant while changing composition.
The hypothesis is intended to apply to room-temperature deformation of identically processed, single-phase FCC alloys.
The proposed behavior may not persist when phase transformations or precipitation occur or when temperature or strain rate changes.
Direct measurement of chemical short-range order and quantitative attribution of its effects on stacking-fault energy and dislocation behavior are challenging.
The magnitude of the proposed chemical-order effects in Cr–Mn–Fe–Co–Ni and its subsets is not precisely constrained.

The hypothesis would be falsified if the quinary alloy lacks significantly greater chemical short-range order or distinct stacking-fault energies and the mechanical differences do not correlate with those features.
